extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society; professional mathematicians, anatomists, and physiologists
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and producing 19th-century Royal Society research reports across mathematics, anatomy, and physiology — emphasizing methodological rigor in hypotheses, proofs, experiments, measurements, and reporting. Suitable for peer reviewers and authors preparing papers for learned societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis-based geometric representation
rubrics_metrics.description: When asking whether quantities (e.g., negative or 'impossible' quantities) can be represented geometrically, the question must be solved by making certain hypotheses respecting their geometric representation and then showing that the results arrived at from these hypotheses are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat definitions and fundamental principles as hypotheses; establish a set of geometric hypotheses (e.g., representation of directed lines, rules for addition, proportion in length and direction), derive algebraic results from them, and demonstrate correctness by logical consequence rather than by appealing only to intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation by agreement with independent processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical hypotheses and definitions are acceptable when the results they produce agree in every respect with results obtained by other independent processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check geometric representations against known algebraic rules and independent methods; mathematicians will be satisfied of correctness when independent lines of reasoning lead to the same results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition defined as composition of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Define addition of directed geometric quantities in the same manner as composition of motion in dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using this definition allows translation of planar dynamical questions (confined to one plane) into algebraic questions; ensure definitions align with physical analogues where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical definition of proportion and multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Four straight lines are proportionals, both in length and direction, when they are proportionals in length and the fourth is inclined to the third at the same angle at which the second is inclined to the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general geometrical definition of proportion/multiplication is necessary to make theories complete; absence of such a definition forces arbitrary limitations in examples and weakens proofs (as noted in criticism of Bue'e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat negative quantities abstractly rather than as mere differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic principles concerning negative quantities should be treated as hypotheses that establish their abstract existence (e.g., directed lines) rather than only as results of subtracting one positive quantity from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid proofs that only apply to the difference of two positive quantities; instead adopt hypotheses about representation and derive algebraic operation rules from them so they hold for negative quantities considered abstractly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing arbitrary limitations to fit examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorists should not introduce ad hoc restrictions into problems merely to make geometrical answers coincide with algebraic roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an author must impose arbitrary limitations for correspondence, this indicates a missing general definition or defect in the theory; seek general definitions rather than tailored examples (criticized in Bue'e's work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor in proving multiplicity of roots (counting roots by dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting that an equation of n dimensions has n roots, provide a rigorous chain of reasoning; do not assume from a figure that each point yields a distinct curve/line without establishing the necessary mapping properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either prove that if a curve surrounds m points then there are m solution lines in that curve, or adopt the standard algebraic technique (show existence of one root then depress the equation to lower degree). Avoid unjustified leaps from premises to conclusions (as noted in critique of Mourey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret imaginary quantities as answers to generalized questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When algebraic solutions yield imaginary quantities, consider that the original question might be expressible in more general terms and that the imaginary quantities are valid answers in that extended sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to interpreting negative algebraic results as meaningful when the question allows, treat imaginary roots as indicating an extension of the question rather than mere impossibility; use this principle to motivate extended formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat experiments until no doubt remains
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental work should be repeated until the result is beyond reasonable doubt in the minds of competent witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproducibility within the original experimental setting is a criterion of reliability; continue trials until observers are convinced of the result's consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct experiments in presence of competent witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: All experiments forming the basis of a claim should be made in the presence of competent witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out experiments with qualified observers to provide verification and to strengthen the credibility of reported results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish only when new facts justify presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should abstain from presenting to learned societies until they have new facts worthy of the society's attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid burdening the society with repetitive or incremental reports; reserve formal presentation for materially new findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine initial reports to simple statement of facts and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: In initial papers, present the facts and the means by which they were ascertained plainly; defer extensive inferential discussion until facts are established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate factual reporting from interpretative synthesis; this improves clarity and allows later papers to supply necessary inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author is suited to review inferences from his own experimental facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquirer, having more perfect knowledge of circumstances and directed attention, is better fitted than others to review the inferences afforded by his facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While facts should be plainly reported, it is acceptable and useful for the original investigator to present the interpretive conclusions, provided they are clearly distinguished from raw data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear definitions and terminology to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Define key terms (e.g., 'ganglion') explicitly for distinction and to avoid circumlocution in exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt simple definitional conventions to improve clarity of argument and avoid repeated long explanations; explicit definitions help readers understand class distinctions used in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek and report independent repetition of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Report whether other physiologists have repeated the experiments and whether they corroborated the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent reproduction by other researchers strengthens the claim; include such citations or notes where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for specimen provenance and social/contextual sampling effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing anatomical specimens shaped by cultural practice (e.g., bound Chinese feet), consider the specimen's provenance and social rank in interpreting how representative or extreme the features are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note possible sampling bias (a specimen from lower ranks may show less extreme deformation than specimens of higher rank); qualify generalizations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate structural observations to functional consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Anatomical descriptions should interpret how morphological changes affect function (e.g., dense cellular tissue implies difficulty in progression; altered heel position changes points of support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect measurements and qualitative observations to likely biomechanical or physiological effects to give the description explanatory value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide precise measurements and positional anatomical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Include exact linear measurements, angles, and relative positions of bones and tissues to describe deformity comprehensively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply numeric lengths/widths/heights and describe axes/relations of bones (e.g., os calcis orientation, distances between articulated points) so others can assess and compare specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate claims about broader significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overstate the importance of a single specimen or finding; present it as interesting or curious but avoid inflating its general relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualify statements about significance and acknowledge limits of inference from single examples; indicate directions for further inquiry rather than sweeping conclusions.
